LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis

Haoxiang Cao   Yuxuan Zhang   Penghui Du   Bo Li   Jiajiong Cao Affiliation: South China Normal University  University of British Columbia    Yingying Fan   Zimeng Wu   Yifu Luo   Mingzhe Zheng   Junwen Miao Affiliation: Vector Institute  Canada CIFAR AI Chair  Carnegie Mellon University Affiliation: University of Waterloo  KlingAI Research  University of Maryland    Huaisong Zhang   Yang Yao   Yu Wang   Dongfu Jiang   Ping Nie Affiliation: Tsinghua University  HKUST  HKU    Wenhu Chen   Chaoqun Wang   Changqian Yu   Kelsey R. Allen Affiliation: South China Normal University  University of British Columbia
Abstract

We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity–relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct–Plan–Exec–Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

1 Introduction

A useful image-generation system [36, 16, 4, 6] should be able to synthesize a new image from the visual evidence provided by the user, even when that evidence is spread across many references. Consider an accessories retailer preparing an advertisement for all handbags with dual parallel top handles (Figure 1). The system must inspect a large inventory, select the relevant bags, reject visually similar distractors, preserve appearance details, and arrange the selected items according to the requested composition. The output may look realistic while still being wrong: it may use the wrong handbag, bind a handle style to the wrong object, violate a count or layout constraint, or introduce unsupported details. The central capability is therefore not visual plausibility alone, but reference-grounded synthesis across retrieval, rejection, binding, and composition.

Evaluating this capability raises a central question: how can we tell whether an image-generation system has synthesized a correct image from long, multi-reference visual context? The difficulty is not only that such tasks contain more images or longer prompts. The required evidence is distributed across references, entities, attributes, relations, hard negatives, unsupported-content rules, and intermediate decisions. Success can only be judged by checking whether the final image satisfies the reference-grounded obligations. A benchmark therefore needs dense multi-reference tasks and scoring that localizes errors rather than a holistic score.

Current image-generation benchmarks [14, 29] capture important parts of this problem, but leave the full measurement target under-specified. Research on instruction-guided editing, personalization, and prompt following addresses local edits and textual requirements [10, 56, 14, 45, 51, 2]. Recent multi-reference benchmarks move closer to reference-based synthesis [23, 37, 3], and automatic evaluation methods support systematic assessment [39, 53, 47]. What remains difficult to measure is dense evidence use: whether the model selected the right references, rejected plausible distractors, attached attributes and relations to the correct entities, and avoided content that is unsupported by either the instruction or the references. A realistic image can pass a surface-level inspection while failing exactly these obligations.

These failures are typically provenance errors rather than rendering errors, where provenance is the source—a specific reference, or the instruction itself—to which each piece of generated content should be attributed: a system may render the right object category while copying appearance from the wrong reference, place the correct entities while violating their relation, or produce a polished composition that leaks a hard negative into the scene. To make such errors measurable, we model each task as an entity–relation graph. Its nodes are the entities, attributes, and text elements that must (or must not) appear; its edges are the spatial, interaction, ordering, and local-appearance relations that bind those entities; and its whole-graph constraints are scene-level obligations—layout, counts, temporal state, and reference selection—that no single node or edge captures. We refer to a node, an edge, or a whole-graph constraint as a graph unit. These three levels define the three graph-grounded scoring dimensions used throughout the paper: Content Fidelity (node level), Relational Binding (edge level), and Global Constraint Satisfaction (whole-graph level). We derive a checklist of atomic, visually verifiable items, each tied to one graph unit, to localize failures.

To make this benchmark auditable at scale, we design LongBanana-Eval, a graph-grounded checklist evaluation pipeline whose scorer LongBananaEval acts as an agentic checklist judge (Section 3): rather than judging the final image with one undifferentiated score, it routes each checklist item to a rubric-guided critic, invokes deterministic tools—OCR, counting, layout, and identity checks—when an item benefits from an executable check, and records evidence traces for quality control and reproducibility. We validate this measurement target on a human-audited pool of 900 generated outputs with 46,700 reviewed checklist labels. An independently double-labeled subset of 7,005 labels (15%) reaches 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted κ\kappa, and these reviewed expert checklist scores serve as the reference standard against which we validate LongBananaEval.

We also use LongBanana to study agent-driven image-generation workflows. Each system wraps a fixed image generator in an agent harness [40, 54, 30]: the harness maintains reference state, selects evidence, schedules prompts, invokes the generator, and revises requests, while the image generator only synthesizes pixels. We evaluate direct generation, minimal agent harnesses, and RPR-enabled harnesses, where RPR is a serial workflow combining ReAct evidence grounding, Plan–Exec decomposition, and Reflect-based revision (Section 4), and we compare multiple image generators under a fixed harness. Across these settings, agent harnesses improve the aggregate profile over direct generation, yet no single harness dominates: the best per-subclass scores remain distributed across direct prompting, minimal harnesses, and RPR. RPR itself yields harness-dependent gains, helping only when the harness reliably exploits retrieved evidence and revision feedback, and otherwise introducing drift.

Contributions

  • •

    Benchmark setting and dataset. We introduce LongBanana-Bench for long-context multi-reference image synthesis, with 90 expert-designed cases, dense references, hard negatives, unsupported-content rules, and a 3×33\times 3 taxonomy.

  • •

    Graph-grounded evaluation. We introduce LongBanana-Eval, mapping entity–relation graphs to atomic checklist items over Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction.

  • •

    Expert verification and audit protocol. We provide reviewed expert checklist labels, agreement statistics, evidence traces, and scorer validation against human labels.

  • •

    Agent-driven generation study. We evaluate direct, harness-based, and RPR workflows to show that current systems fail in structured, diagnosable ways rather than along a single image-quality axis.

2 The LongBanana Benchmark

2.1 Goal and Scope

LongBanana is an evaluation benchmark for long-horizon multi-reference image synthesis. A system is given a heterogeneous reference set and a structured synthesis instruction, and must render one coherent image that satisfies the obligations of the task’s entity–relation graph (Section 1): its required and forbidden nodes, the edges that bind them, and the whole-graph constraints on the scene. The setting differs from low-reference editing because the decisive evidence is distributed across many images, and correctness is measured by the graph-derived checklist of atomic, visually verifiable items rather than by a single holistic quality score. LongBanana contains 90 cases: 10 cases for each subclass in a 3×33\times 3 taxonomy. A typical case contains approximately 32 references and more than 20 cross-reference constraints, and across the benchmark experts specify 4,670 atomic checklist items. Because every item is tied to a single graph unit, each failure is localized to a specific obligation rather than absorbed into an overall score.

2.2 Task Taxonomy and Evaluation Rubric

We organize LongBanana tasks into a three-suite taxonomy that captures their primary synthesis demands (Figure 2). Across these tasks, a shared graph-grounded rubric evaluates whether the generated image preserves the required content, relations, and scene-level constraints.

The three suites are Scene Composition (semantic coverage, relational graph consistency, and layout arrangement), Visual Appearance (global appearance conditioning, local appearance binding, and appearance harmonization), and Reference Reasoning (selection and retrieval, temporal/state reasoning, and counting/aggregation). All tasks require a final image output; subclasses differ in the evidence-integration behavior being tested.

For each case, checklist items assess correctness at three levels of the entity–relation graph: nodes, edges, and the whole graph. Content Fidelity measures node-level correctness: required entities, attributes, text elements, and supported semantic nodes must appear, while forbidden or unsupported nodes must be absent. Relational Binding measures edge-level correctness, including spatial relations, interactions, ordering, support, containment, and local bindings such as texture, material, color, pose, or state assigned to a specific entity. Global Constraint Satisfaction measures whole-graph correctness, including composition, layout, scene-level style, count and aggregation constraints, temporal/state constraints, and reference-selection constraints.

This graph-grounded rubric localizes failures to specific content, bindings, or scene-level obligations, supporting consistent diagnosis across task categories and generation systems.

2.3 Benchmark Construction

We construct each case around a shared entity–relation graph that connects the synthesis instruction, reference images, and evaluation checklist (Figure 3). Construction proceeds from a scenario description to structured constraints, then to the visual references and instruction that express the task, and finally to the checklist used to evaluate its result.

Scenario and graph construction.

Expert authors design scenarios aligned with the task taxonomy, drawing on storyboard, product, and scene-composition use cases. A scenario specifies what the final image should depict and which entities, visual attributes, and interactions must be preserved. An LLM then structures the scenario into an entity–relation graph: nodes represent entities and their attributes, edges encode spatial relations, interactions, and local appearance bindings, and whole-graph constraints specify requirements such as composition and counts. This representation makes the dependencies explicit. For example, an appearance requirement identifies both the visual property and the entity to which it belongs, while a relational requirement identifies the entities that must participate in the requested configuration. These constraints guide both task synthesis and checklist derivation.

Instruction and reference construction.

The graph guides the creation of the target instruction and reference images, including entity, appearance, and optional background references. The instruction expresses the requested composition and the relationships to be realized; the references supply the visual identities, local details, and appearance cues needed to instantiate it. Discriminative visual attributes are retained in the references and omitted from text where possible. Because these cues are distributed across images, the generator must associate each relevant reference with the intended graph entity and combine their evidence while maintaining the requested relations. At least 30 cases also include two or more hard-negative references that are visually plausible but irrelevant to the requested output. Their exclusion is encoded in the checklist, allowing distractor leakage to be assessed alongside the inclusion of required content.

Checklist derivation.

We translate graph constraints into atomic checklist items using the rubric introduced in Section 2.2. Node-level items check required entities and attributes; edge-level items check relations and appearance bindings; whole-graph items check scene-wide requirements such as layout and counts. Each item records an observable condition, the graph unit it evaluates, the relevant reference images, and its scoring criteria. This links a judgment about the output to the evidence needed to make it. Positive items test whether a required condition is satisfied, while negative items check for the absence of distractor or unsupported content. Each completed case therefore pairs an instruction and reference set with a checklist derived from the same task constraints. Section 3 describes how these items are scored.

Case curation.

Human curators review the instruction, reference images, and checklist together, checking their correspondence to the task graph. They inspect whether the references visibly support the required identities and attributes, whether the requested relations and composition are visually feasible, and whether checklist items express clear, individually verifiable conditions. They also check reference density, constraint coverage, and overlapping or ambiguous items. Requirements that cannot be judged from the references and a candidate output are revised or rejected before inclusion. Appendix B provides the detailed construction protocol and case specifications. Section 4 describes human labeling of generated outputs to establish reference judgments for evaluator validation.

3 LongBanana-Eval: Graph-Grounded Checklist Evaluation

LongBanana-Eval evaluates a generated image against the case’s graph-derived checklist. Its agentic checklist judge, LongBananaEval, prepares item-specific reference evidence, routes each check to a dimension-specific critic, and combines the resulting judgments into dimension-level and overall scores. As shown in Figure 4, the pipeline also records the evidence supporting each item judgment.

3.1 Checklist Scoring Protocol

Evidence preparation and routing.

For each item, the parser reads the condition to verify, its rubric dimension, reference identifiers, and scoring criteria from the case specification. It assembles the generated image and relevant reference images into an evidence packet, with optional crops to localize the region under inspection. Negative-content checks additionally receive the identifiers and roles of applicable hard-negative references. The router assigns the packet to the critic corresponding to the item’s rubric dimension.

Dimension-specific checks and tools.

The Content Fidelity critic checks required entities, attributes, and text, together with the absence of forbidden or distractor content. The Relational Binding critic checks spatial and interaction relations and the assignment of local appearance cues to their intended entities. The Global Constraint Satisfaction critic checks scene-wide requirements, including layout, global style, counts, and temporal or state constraints. Each critic compares the output with the item’s reference evidence and may invoke verification tools: OCR for readable text, detection or counting for multiplicity, layout routines for spatial constraints, and identity or feature matching for consistency. The critic combines these observations with the visual evidence to determine whether the item is satisfied.

Item judgments and evidence traces.

Each check produces a label sj∈{0,1,2}s_{j}\in\{0,1,2\}: 22 for a satisfied requirement, 11 for partial satisfaction or uncertain evidence, and 00 for an unsatisfied requirement. For negative items, the requirement is the absence of forbidden or unsupported content: complete absence scores 22, ambiguous or suspicious leakage scores 11, and clear erroneous appearance scores 00. The evidence trace associates the label with the relevant references, the critic’s findings, and any tool observations. Traces are organized by the same three rubric dimensions, linking each reported judgment to the evidence used to reach it.

Score aggregation.

For a generated image with NN checklist items, the overall score is the mean item label scaled to 00–1010. Dimension scores apply the same calculation to the item set JdJ_{d} assigned to dimension dd:

Soverall=5N​∑j=1Nsj,Sd=5|Jd|​∑j∈Jdsj.S_{\mathrm{overall}}=\frac{5}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}s_{j},\qquad S_{d}=\frac{5}{|J_{d}|}\sum_{j\in J_{d}}s_{j}.

The dimension scores provide a diagnostic profile, while the overall score summarizes the full checklist. The main generation tables express checklist-average scores on a 00–100100 scale; Section 4 separately defines the difficulty-weighted task pass rate, P@70%.

Baseline and validation.

The VLM-as-judge baseline receives the generated image, relevant references, and checklist in a single judging call and returns item labels for the same score aggregation. It shares the judging backbone and item-level criteria with LongBananaEval, whose execution organizes evidence and tool use around individual checks. Section 4 evaluates both judges against reviewed human labels at the item and output-score levels; implementation details appear in Appendix C.

4 Experiments

Our experiments connect evaluator validation with a study of long-context image generation. We first establish agreement between automatic checklist judgments and reviewed human labels. We then ask how much explicit graph structure helps a non-agentic generator, what adaptive agentic workflows add beyond an optimized static plan, and how those gains interact with the image backend.

4.1 Protocol and Metrics

Generation conditions.

We evaluate all systems on the held-out 90-case LongBanana benchmark. Table 2 fixes Nano Banana 2 and compares two direct baselines, three minimal agent harnesses, and their RPR-enabled variants. Table 3 fixes OpenClaw + RPR and compares three image backends. The shared OpenClaw + RPR with Nano Banana 2 configuration connects the two comparisons, yielding ten distinct generation conditions.

FP-Direct (full-prompt direct) keeps the full target prompt fixed and slides an eight-reference window over the inventory. PD-Direct (prompt-decomposed direct) tests how far non-agentic generation can go with explicit task structure and optimal composition scheduling. We give it privileged access to the entity–relation graph used to construct each case, including entity-to-reference correspondences. Under the same eight-reference backend budget as FP-Direct, it batches graph nodes and constructs relation-aware prompts. Its prompts expose relations incident to each batch, and each generated intermediate becomes the input for the next composition step. Integer programming solves the staging schedule exactly: first maximize relations whose anchors are composed no later than their dependents, then minimize total relational stretch ∑(u,v)∈E|b⁡(u)−b⁡(v)|\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\lvert b(u)-b(v)\rvert, where b⁡(⋅)b(\cdot) is the batch index. PD-Direct thus exploits the construction graph through a fixed, optimized execution plan; the agentic systems do not receive this graph or the evaluation checklist.

The agentic conditions use Hermes-Agent, OpenCode, and OpenClaw, with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as their shared agent model. A minimal harness maintains reference state, organizes prompts, calls the image backend, and records revisions. RPR coordinates three stages: ReAct retrieves and reasons over reference evidence; Plan–Exec decomposes the grounded request into generation or editing steps; and Reflect lets the agent inspect drafts and decide on further retrieval or revision. Appendix D provides the direct-baseline and workflow implementations.

Human reference labels.

The human evaluation pool (the audit pool) covers all 90 benchmark cases under 10 generation conditions, yielding 90×10=90090\times 10=900 generated outputs. The case-specific checklists contain 4,670 items in total across the 90 cases. Applying each case’s checklist to its outputs under all 10 conditions produces 4,670×10=46,7004{,}670\times 10=46{,}700 item-level judgments, for which human annotators provide reviewed labels.

Human labels undergo primary annotation, second-pass review, and expert adjudication. To assess annotator consistency, 15% of the item-level judgments—46,700×0.15=7,00546{,}700\times 0.15=7{,}005—receive independent labels from two annotators. On this subset, exact label agreement is 89.4%, and quadratic weighted κ\kappa is 0.83. Appendix B provides the annotation protocol, audit-correction results, and rank-stability analyses.

Generation scoring.

The subclass and Overall Avg. columns measure the extent of constraint satisfaction through the unweighted checklist-average score. Each item label sj∈{0,1,2}s_{j}\in\{0,1,2\} is normalized as rj=sj/2r_{j}=s_{j}/2, and the mean normalized label over the relevant checklist items is expressed on a 00–100100 scale. The subclass columns follow the nine task categories; Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction provide the complementary item-level grading axis.

P@70% measures task-level coverage: the percentage of the 90 case–subclass tasks whose difficulty-weighted score reaches 70. Each case contributes one task in its primary subclass. For strategy aa and task tt,

TaskScore⁡(a,t)=100⋅∑j∈twj​ra,j∑j∈twj.\mathrm{TaskScore}(a,t)=100\cdot\frac{\sum_{j\in t}w_{j}r_{a,j}}{\sum_{j\in t}w_{j}}.

For the main comparisons, each item’s difficulty weight wjw_{j} is computed once from human scores for a fixed reference-system pool, versioned, and held fixed for subsequent systems. The overall average therefore summarizes checklist fulfillment, while P@70% highlights how often a system reaches the task-level threshold with greater emphasis on difficult requirements. Together, they reveal whether an improvement is spread across checklist items or carries more tasks past the threshold. Appendix C.4 specifies the weighting rule and aggregation details.

4.2 Evaluator Validation

Judge–human agreement.

Table 1 compares the single-pass VLM-as-judge baseline and LongBananaEval, our agentic checklist judge, against the 900 audit-pool outputs with 46,700 reviewed human labels. Both judges use Gemini 3 Flash and produce item labels under the scoring protocol of Section 3. We report Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlations between judge checklist-derived overall scores s^o\hat{s}_{o} and reviewed expert overall scores sos_{o}. Because this pool covers every case and every reported generation condition, these agreement measures test whether automatic judges preserve expert score trends across the complete reported output set, and provide the validation basis for reporting LongBananaEval machine scores in Tables 2 and 3.

The agentic checklist judge achieves higher agreement on all three output-level correlation measures. At the item level, it also increases exact ternary agreement by 15.82 percentage points and reduces opposite-end 0↔20\leftrightarrow 2 errors by 19.28 points (Table 10). Output-level correlations establish closer alignment with expert score trends, while the item-level comparison shows improved decisions about individual requirements. These complementary results support using LongBananaEval to measure generation performance and produce evidence-linked diagnostic reports.

4.3 Generation Results and Analysis

Generation result pattern.

Table 2 establishes PD-Direct as a strong non-agentic baseline. Graph-informed staging substantially improves on FP-Direct, with the best Global Appearance Conditioning (GAC) score and the second-best Layout Arrangement Consistency (LAC) score across all compared systems. Its improvements also extend to local appearance binding, reference selection, and aggregation. These results demonstrate the practical value of exploiting known task structure: organizing entities and their relations into a precomputed composition schedule can support competitive multi-reference synthesis. The direct baseline remains competitive on these subclasses even against systems equipped with retrieval and reflection. PD-Direct’s strengths make the subsequent agentic comparison meaningful, since its task structure is supplied directly and its scheduling objective is solved exactly.

Agentic systems nevertheless achieve broader success without direct access to the construction graph. Most agentic configurations exceed PD-Direct in overall average, and OpenClaw + RPR surpasses it on eight of nine subclasses, with a 3.8-point average-score gain and a 12.2-percentage-point gain in task pass rate. This advantage reaches beyond scene composition to reference selection, state reasoning, and aggregation. The comparison exposes a gap between knowing the intended constraint structure and realizing it through successive image-generation steps. The graph specifies desired relations, while intermediate images reveal which constraints have actually survived the latest generation step. A fixed graph schedule organizes what should be composed; adaptive workflows can additionally inspect evidence, maintain reference bindings, and revise execution as synthesis unfolds. Their advantage over a structurally privileged baseline provides strong evidence for the value of agentic orchestration in long-context image generation.

Within the agentic configurations, RPR gives OpenClaw the strongest overall average and a joint-best task pass rate. Its clearest improvements over the minimal harness occur in scene composition, reference selection, and aggregation, consistent with a workflow that links evidence acquisition to execution and repair. The minimal OpenClaw harness remains stronger on temporal and state reasoning. OpenCode and Hermes-Agent also improve their average scores with RPR, while their task pass rates decline. These profiles identify reliable coordination as the next design priority: retrieved evidence must remain attached to the correct entities and constraints through planning, generation, and revision.

Workflow component analysis.

The RPR ablation in Table 11 isolates retrieval, planning, and reflection with OpenClaw and Nano Banana 2 fixed. Plan–Exec alone is strongest on global appearance conditioning and local appearance binding; ReAct alone improves reference selection over the minimal harness; and Reflect alone improves layout, aggregation, and task pass rate. The full workflow achieves the strongest overall result and pass rate among the component variants.

These profiles give a concrete direction for agent design. Evidence retrieval supplies the relevant references, planning organizes their use, and reflection checks the realized composition against the task. Their combined workflow turns these operations into a coordinated generation process, extending the benefits of decomposition with evidence inspection and feedback. The component results reinforce the main comparison: static organization is useful, and its integration with grounding and repair produces the strongest overall configuration in this study.

Image-backend comparison.

With OpenClaw + RPR fixed, Nano Banana 2 leads across all nine subclasses (Table 3). Seedream 4 is stronger than GPT Image 1 on scene composition, temporal and state reasoning, and aggregation, whereas GPT Image 1 is more competitive on visual appearance and reference selection. The fixed workflow makes these differences informative about each backend’s ability to realize reference-grounded instructions.

Backend capability and agentic orchestration offer complementary paths to improvement. The harness controls evidence selection, constraint organization, and revision, while the image model determines how faithfully these decisions become pixels. A stronger workflow improves the use of the available visual evidence; a stronger backend improves its realization in the generated image. The broad Nano Banana 2 advantage shows that backend capability remains consequential even under the strongest evaluated workflow.

Diagnostic implications.

The comparison with PD-Direct highlights the distinction between planning a composition and controlling its realization. PD-Direct uses privileged graph information to optimize reference grouping and ordering, then executes that schedule in stages. The resulting images can still depart from the intended constraints as entities are added or edited. Agentic workflows can inspect intermediate outputs, revisit reference evidence, and adjust subsequent actions. Their broader advantage motivates treating the evolving visual state, alongside the task structure, as central to generation control.

The checklist turns this control problem into inspectable requirements. PD-Direct’s strong appearance conditioning alongside its weaker reference selection and state reasoning directs attention to evidence use across composition steps. Item judgments and evidence traces can distinguish an incorrect reference choice from an incorrect entity binding or an unmet scene-wide requirement. For future agent designs, these diagnostics offer a basis for choosing what to revisit and what to preserve during revision. The resulting research target is evidence-guided adaptation: connect inspection of the current image to the next retrieval, generation, or repair action while preserving satisfied constraints.

Further analyses.

Appendix D reports the workflow ablation and case-paired score diagnostics. The generation comparisons, component study, and item-level traces together connect aggregate performance to the decisions made during synthesis, providing a basis for developing more capable reference-grounded image-generation agents.

5 Conclusion

LongBanana establishes long-context multi-reference image synthesis as a benchmark for integrating dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, and satisfying coupled content and relational constraints. LongBanana-Bench provides 90 expert-designed and expert-verified cases across a 3×33\times 3 taxonomy, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. LongBanana-Eval turns these constraints into evidence-linked judgments, validated against human labels, to measure constraint fulfillment and localize generation failures.

The generation study highlights the distinction between optimizing a composition plan and adaptively controlling its realization. PD-Direct combines privileged access to the construction graph with exactly optimized staging, establishing a competitive non-agentic baseline. Agentic workflows achieve broader success without direct access to that graph, showing the value of adaptive evidence use and generation control beyond a fixed schedule. The RPR component study further supports coordinating retrieval, execution, and repair within one workflow. These findings point toward agents that reason over both task structure and the evolving visual state, preserve reference bindings across steps, and target unmet requirements during revision.

Appendix A Related Work

Image Synthesis Benchmarks.

Image-generation benchmarks cover instruction-guided editing, personalization, human alignment, and reasoning-oriented synthesis [48, 29, 28, 22, 46, 24] but generally focus on creating a single image from a single prompt. Recent multi-reference benchmarks [23, 37, 42, 3] are closer to our setting, but they typically use fewer references or lower-density cross-image constraints. LongBanana targets final-image synthesis in which correctness depends on retrieving, rejecting, binding, and integrating evidence distributed across dozens of references.

Atomic Constraint Evaluation.

Long-context tasks have long been a central challenge across language and vision domains [23, 1, 41, 18, 19]. Instruction-following benchmarks in NLP often convert open-ended tasks into verifiable atomic requirements. IFEval [55] emphasizes directly checkable constraints, and TIFA [11] converts text-to-image faithfulness into question-answer checks. LongBanana transfers this principle to long-horizon multi-reference synthesis. Each checklist item links the output to a graph node, graph edge, or whole-graph constraint, so failures can be traced to missing content, incorrect relations, hard-negative leakage, unsupported content, or global constraint violations.

Automatic Judges.

Low-level metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [12, 35, 49] are poorly matched to reference faithfulness, motivating model-based judges and rubric evaluators [5, 9, 15, 43, 20, 33, 44, 26, 52, 53, 38, 7, 58, 27, 8, 57]. However, a holistic judge can conflate realism with correctness when many references are present [21, 32, 34, 50, 17]. LongBananaEval evaluates checklist-level evidence with routed critics and tools, and we report its validity through Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall agreement with reviewed expert labels [31, 25, 13].

Appendix B Benchmark and Dataset Details

B.1 Detailed Taxonomy

Table 4 gives the full 3×33\times 3 taxonomy used to organize LongBanana. The suites separate scene composition, visual appearance, and reference reasoning demands, while the subclasses specify the dominant checklist requirement for each group of cases.

B.2 Construction Rationale

Table 5 expands the construction choices summarized in Section 2.

B.3 Benchmark Statistics

Table 6 summarizes the fixed benchmark scale and annotation load. These quantities describe the benchmark design itself, including the number of suites, cases, references, constraints, checklist items, and hard-negative settings, rather than model performance.

B.4 Benchmark Comparison

Table 7 positions LongBanana relative to representative image-editing and image-synthesis benchmarks. The comparison emphasizes why LongBanana targets long-horizon multi-reference synthesis: dense reference sets, many cross-reference constraints, atomic checklist evaluation, and explicit human-label quality control.

B.5 Asset Provenance, Licenses, and Consent

Each source image or generated asset is tracked with source, creator when known, access date, intended use, redistribution status, and privacy/safety screening status. Assets with uncertain provenance, personal-data concerns, unsafe content, or incompatible redistribution terms are excluded from unrestricted release or handled through controlled access.

B.6 Evaluation Specification Schema

Each case serializes the evaluation specification in a machine-readable schema:

  • •

    Case fields: case_id, suite, subclass, instruction, reference_inventory, evidence_graph (the entity–relation graph), hard_negative_references, unsupported_content_rules, checklist_items, rubric_dimensions, and provenance_status.

  • •

    Checklist-item fields: item_id, dimension, graph_unit, polarity, required_references, observable_condition, label_set, and human_evidence_notes.

  • •

    Rubric dimensions: content_fidelity, relational_binding, and global_constraint_satisfaction.

B.7 Checklist Item Template

A checklist item is valid only if it is visually verifiable, reference-grounded, and non-redundant where possible. Positive items evaluate whether a required fact is present and correctly bound. Negative items are Content Fidelity checks that evaluate whether a distractor or unsupported element is absent: completely absent is labeled 2, visually suspicious or ambiguous leakage is labeled 1, and full erroneous appearance is labeled 0. Items requiring specialist interpretation include a short reference note identifying the evidence to inspect.

B.8 Annotation Interface and Protocol

Annotators view the reference set, target instruction, generated output, checklist item evidence, and explicit 0/1/2 scoring instructions. The human-audited multi-system output pool covers all 90 cases and all 10 reported generation conditions, yielding 900 generated outputs. Human reviewers assign 46,700 reviewed checklist labels by applying all 4,670 benchmark checklist items to every reported condition. The three rubric dimensions are computed from the corresponding checklist labels. The protocol uses primary annotation, second-pass review, third-pass expert adjudication, an independently double-labeled subset of 7,005 labels, stratified audit sampling, schema validation, and score-stability checks. The annotation audit records include qualification and training criteria, review status, correction logs, adjudication logs, audit outcomes, and stability summaries without exposing annotator identities. Figures 5 and 6 show screenshots from the checklist annotation platform used for these human reviews.

B.9 Expert Label Quality Control

Table 8 summarizes label quality control. All 46,700 judgments undergo review and adjudication, with difficult items receiving further review to establish final labels. Errors found in the random audit trigger expanded checks of related labels, and the label set is frozen after all revisions. Table 9 compares scores and rankings for the same ten generation conditions across label versions using the same checklist-average aggregation.

B.10 Human Annotation Platform and Audit Trail

Figures 5 and 6 show representative checklist-item screens from the human annotation platform. Each item is evaluated as an atomic visual verification task rather than as a holistic image preference: the annotator sees the target image, the relevant reference images, the generation prompt, the item-specific question, labeling guidance, option definitions, and the allowed ternary labels. The platform records the case metadata, checklist category, label result identifier, annotator submission, timestamp, selected score, and review outcome. Final labels are accepted only after the review/adjudication process described above, yielding an auditable item-level trail for the 46,700 human-reviewed checklist labels used in the judge validation.

Appendix C LongBanana-Eval Details

C.1 LLM and Agent Usage Declaration

LongBananaEval uses LLM or MLLM components as rubric critics, tool routers, and evidence-analysis modules. All automatic judging runs use Gemini 3 Flash as the shared judging backbone for both the agentic checklist judge and the single-pass VLM judge; in the agentic checklist judge, Gemini 3 Flash also drives tool routing and evidence analysis. LongBanana-Gen uses OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Hermes-Agent as harnesses. All three harnesses use Claude Sonnet 4.6 as the shared underlying agent model for planning, tool selection, and prompt revision. The harness versions are Hermes-Agent 0.10.0, OpenCode 1.4.9, and OpenClaw 2026.4.16. These harnesses call reference browsing, OCR/count/layout, image-generation, and file or prompt-management tools, while Nano Banana 2, GPT Image 1, or Seedream 4 produces image pixels according to the experimental setting.

C.2 Human Agreement and Opposite-End Error Reduction

The full-pool comparison uses all 46,700 reviewed checklist decisions from 900 generated outputs across 10 generation conditions. We compare VLM-as-judge with LongBananaEval against the reviewed human labels. Each atomic check uses 22 for satisfied/correct, 11 for partially satisfied or uncertain, and 00 for unsatisfied/incorrect; when absence is required, correct omission scores 22. For a human label yy and evaluator label y^\hat{y}, exact ternary agreement requires y^=y\hat{y}=y, within-one agreement requires |y^−y|≤1|\hat{y}-y|\leq 1, and opposite-end error occurs when |y^−y|=2|\hat{y}-y|=2.

Table 10 shows that exact ternary agreement increases by 15.82 percentage points, from 50.99% to 66.81%, while within-one agreement increases by 19.28 points, from 55.91% to 75.19%. Opposite-end 0↔20\leftrightarrow 2 errors decrease from 44.09% to 24.81%, reducing complete satisfaction–failure reversals by 19.28 points. Within-one agreement and opposite-end error are complementary for ternary labels, so these two changes describe the same reduction in severe errors. These item-level results complement the output-level score correlations in Table 1 and support finer-grained diagnosis of reference-grounded failures.

C.3 Tool Configuration and Aggregation

The tool inventory covers OCR, object counting or detection, layout checking, and identity or feature matching. Tool calls produce observations rather than final labels. Item judgments use item-specific labels in {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}; for negative Content Fidelity items, absence is pass = 2, suspicious or ambiguous leakage is partial = 1, and full erroneous appearance is fail = 0. Checklist-average diagnostics multiply the mean label by 5, yielding a 0–10 score (rescaled to 0–100 for the subclass and Overall Avg. columns of the main generation tables) used for judge agreement and the main checklist-average columns; in the main generation tables, difficulty weighting is used only for the P@70% column. No polarity inversion is applied after labeling.

C.4 Difficulty-Weighted Generation Scoring

The P@70% column of the main generation tables uses a difficulty-weighted checklist score computed at the case–subclass task level; the subclass and Overall Avg. columns instead report the unweighted checklist-average score (the per-item mean rescaled to 0–100). Each checklist judgment is first mapped to a ternary item score sj∈{0,1,2}s_{j}\in\{0,1,2\}: pass/match/correct is 2, partial satisfaction or uncertainty is 1, and fail/mismatch/incorrect/invalid is 0. Let rj=sj/2r_{j}=s_{j}/2 be the normalized item score. We calibrate difficulty once using the reviewed human labels for the fixed reference pool of ten generation conditions. For each checklist item key (case,subclass,item)(\mathrm{case},\mathrm{subclass},\mathrm{item}), qjq_{j} is the mean normalized human label over this reference pool, defining the difficulty weight

wj={3,qj<0.65,2,0.65≤qj<0.90,1,qj≥0.90.w_{j}=\begin{cases}3,&q_{j}<0.65,\\ 2,&0.65\leq q_{j}<0.90,\\ 1,&q_{j}\geq 0.90.\end{cases}

The resulting weight map is saved as a versioned benchmark configuration and used unchanged in the main comparisons and for subsequent benchmark systems. The task score for strategy aa on case–subclass task tt is

TaskScore⁡(a,t)=100⋅∑j∈twj​sa,j∑j∈t2​wj=100⋅∑j∈twj​ra,j∑j∈twj.\mathrm{TaskScore}(a,t)=100\cdot\frac{\sum_{j\in t}w_{j}s_{a,j}}{\sum_{j\in t}2w_{j}}=100\cdot\frac{\sum_{j\in t}w_{j}r_{a,j}}{\sum_{j\in t}w_{j}}.

P@70% is the percentage of the 90 case–subclass tasks whose weighted score is at least 70; each benchmark case contributes one task in its primary subclass. The subclass and Overall Avg. columns of the main tables instead report the unweighted checklist-average score over the same tasks. For judge–human agreement, we separately use output-level checklist-average scores

so=5⋅1no∑j=1noyo,j,s^o=5⋅1no∑j=1noy^o,j,s_{o}=5\cdot\frac{1}{n_{o}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{o}}y_{o,j},\qquad\hat{s}_{o}=5\cdot\frac{1}{n_{o}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{o}}\hat{y}_{o,j},

to correlate reviewed labels yy with judge predictions y^\hat{y} over the 900-output human-audited pool.

Appendix D Additional Generation Experiments and Diagnostics

Figure 17 visualizes the two main result comparisons from Tables 2 and 3. The radar profiles are intended as compact diagnostics of subclass-level failure patterns, not as additional statistical tests.

D.1 Direct Baseline Implementations

FP-Direct uses the full target prompt throughout generation and varies only the visible reference window. Because a case may contain more reference images than the backend can consume at once, the implementation uses a window of eight references and iterates over the ordered reference inventory, e.g., ref1--ref8, ref9--ref16, and so on until all non-background references have been exposed. Each round receives the same complete target prompt; there is no entity-level batching, graph-conditioned relation filtering, explicit state memory, or repair step.

PD-Direct is a deterministic staged-composition baseline rather than a free-form planning agent. It uses the same eight-reference backend budget as FP-Direct, but allocates that budget by graph structure rather than by inventory order. Each non-background entity node is represented by one reference image. Starting from the pre-generated background image, PD-Direct composes non-background entities in ordered batches of at most eight entity references, following the staging schedule that is optimal for the case’s entity–relation graph. Let b⁡(v)∈{1,…,K}b(v)\in\{1,\dots,K\} be the batch index of entity vv, with K=⌈N/8⌉K=\lceil N/8\rceil, at most eight entity references per batch, and the background fixed at batch 00. Over the (unweighted, directed, possibly cyclic) entity–relation graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), the schedule minimizes a lexicographic objective: first the number of relations (u,v)(u,v) whose anchor is composed later than its dependent, |{(u,v)∈E:b⁡(u)>b⁡(v)}|\lvert\{(u,v)\in E:b(u)>b(v)\}\rvert, a capacity-constrained feedback-arc count that we minimize exactly by integer programming, and, among schedules attaining that minimum, the total relational stretch ∑(u,v)∈E|b⁡(u)−b⁡(v)|\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\lvert b(u)-b(v)\rvert. We solve it exactly with an integer program (Pass 1 minimizes the feedback count F⋆F^{\star}; Pass 2 minimizes the stretch subject to the feedback count equal to F⋆F^{\star}); each case has a small number of composed entities (N≤32N\leq 32), so the integer program solves in seconds. At step zero the backend receives the background image plus the first batch’s reference images and produces intermediate_00.png; at each later step it receives the previous intermediate image plus the next batch’s references, and the final intermediate is saved as target/target_image.png. For a case with N=32N=32 composed entities this yields K=⌈N/8⌉=4K=\lceil N/8\rceil=4 batches and four intermediate images. The prompt at each step is constructed deterministically from fixed staged-composition instructions, the scene prompt, the entity types in the current batch, and all graph edges incident to that batch (there is no per-step cap on edges, so every relation is presented at the step of its later endpoint), followed by constraints to preserve existing content and maintain consistent lighting, scale, and perspective. Reference images and the background are generated upstream from the entity catalog, scene specification, and entity–relation graph; PD-Direct only stages their use during target construction.

D.2 Agent-Orchestrator Component Ablation

Figure 18 summarizes the ReAct, Plan–Exec, and Reflect stages used by the full RPR workflow. Table 11 isolates these stages with OpenClaw and Nano Banana 2 fixed, comparing the minimal OpenClaw harness, each single-stage variant, and the full OpenClaw + RPR stack. For this ablation, item difficulty is computed from the mean normalized item score across the five configurations in this table, using the thresholds in Appendix C.4. The resulting weights are shared across all five rows. Subclass scores, Overall Avg., and P@70% therefore use this within-table relative difficulty calibration rather than the main benchmark’s frozen reference-pool weights.

The ablation shows that the three agentic stages are complementary rather than individually monotonic. Plan–Exec alone gives the strongest Visual Appearance scores on GAC and LAB, consistent with decomposition helping product, style, and material organization, but it weakens relation control and structured reasoning when evidence retrieval and repair are not coupled to the plan. ReAct alone improves selection relative to the minimal OpenClaw harness, but its overall score drops because evidence selection without explicit execution control does not reliably preserve spatial and appearance bindings through generation. Reflect alone raises LAC, AGG, and P@70%, indicating that revision helps repair visible layout and aggregation errors, but it can also over-correct or drift when missing evidence is not re-grounded.

The full RPR stack gives the best overall score and pass rate because the stages close each other’s failure modes: ReAct grounds the reference set, Plan–Exec turns the grounded state into an executable synthesis schedule, and Reflect supports revision based on the generated result. The remaining TSR drop relative to minimal OpenClaw suggests that temporal and state-reasoning cases are sensitive to over-revision: once a physically plausible final state is found, additional repair can shift pose or event timing away from the intended state. Thus, RPR is best interpreted as an evidence-preserving orchestration pattern, not as a uniformly beneficial amount of extra reasoning.

D.3 Case-Level Uncertainty and Paired Inference on the Checklist-Average Score

Appendix E Responsible Release and Safeguards

E.1 Limitations

The 3×33\times 3 taxonomy covers a meaningful subset of long-horizon multi-reference synthesis, but does not cover video generation, 3D scene composition, or unrestricted multimodal planning. The benchmark is intentionally high-density, which improves diagnostic resolution but makes expert annotation expensive. LongBananaEval depends on backbone multimodal models and verification tools, so model identifiers and tool versions must accompany final results.

E.2 Broader Impact Details

The benchmark is designed for measurement rather than deployment, but it evaluates systems capable of generating realistic composite images from many references. Positive uses include model auditing and failure diagnosis. Risks include deceptive media, impersonation, privacy leakage, biased reference coverage, and copyright-sensitive reuse. Mitigations include filtering unsafe content, documenting provenance, restricting problematic assets, and providing a project issue tracker for reporting release problems at https://github.com/TIGER-AI-Lab/LongBanana/issues.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and Section 1 state the benchmark, evaluator, and empirical claims, while Sections 2, 3, 4 and 5 define the scope and required evidence. Run-specific factual details are provided in the anonymized OpenReview artifacts and associated run records.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Appendix E discusses benchmark scope, annotation expense, and evaluator dependence.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: The paper does not present theoretical theorems or formal proof claims.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [No]

  19. Justification: The paper describes benchmark construction, scoring, model and harness identifiers, and baseline implementations in Sections 2, 3, 4, B, C and D, but does not include executable reproduction commands or environment files.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [No]

  24. Justification: This preprint does not provide a public data/code access link with executable reproduction instructions.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  29. Justification: The experimental design, 90-case benchmark, evaluator configuration, metrics, and ablations are described in Sections 2, 3 and 4. Appendix C identifies the agent and judging models and the harness versions.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Section 4 reports checklist-average generation scores and the secondary difficulty-weighted P@70% diagnostic. Appendix D reports case-level bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests for the checklist-average scores; judge–human agreement is reported as correlation diagnostics.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: Appendix E discusses positive impacts for evaluation rigor and negative risks related to deceptive media, privacy, copyright, and biased coverage, together with mitigation measures.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).
